sections.title: Employment Contract
sections.text:
Styopa Razin, leader of the independent tactical legion 'Shchin', seeks a brief clasp of hands with the one who has caught his eye.

Cooperation, not subordination. He draws that line clearly now.

sections.title: Token
sections.text: A golden medal. On the blue enamel ring at its center, the words "Faith and Loyalty" are engraved in Ursus script. He has never believed in any of it.

sections.title: Profile
sections.text: Styopa Razin, leader and commander-in-chief of the Ursus independent tactical legion "Shchin," and a leader of the Freemen. In early 1102 he led his men out from under the jurisdiction of the Ursus military, and after the Deity Grypherburg Incident, broke away entirely. He later began making contact with Rhodes Island on "Shchin's" behalf, through an introduction from an operator at one of our offices.

sections.title: Clinical Analysis
sections.text:
Imaging tests reveal clear, normal outlines of internal organs, and no abnormal shadows have been detected. Originium granules have not been detected in the circulatory system and there is no sign of infection. At this time, this operator is believed to be uninfected.

[Cell-Originium Assimilation] 0%
Operator Viy shows no signs of Originium infection.

[Blood Originium-Crystal Density] 0.19u/L
Given how widely the readings fluctuate, even taking nothing but the final average still yields a rather dangerous figure. Continued observation is advised.
The problem may lie with the Arts Unit Operator Viy uses. It houses a complex Originium circuit that defies any conventional analysis on our part—perhaps the product of some Ursus military research, or perhaps an unrecorded tradition of the "Freemen." All we know at present is that this circuit amplifies the energy of the Originium embedded in the Arts Unit to an extreme level, so as to obtain the best possible Arts effect. In exchange, an Arts Unit of this kind places an enormous burden on the caster's body; the slightest carelessness can cause irreversible nerve damage, or even leave the caster with Oripathy. If at all possible, we hope Operator Viy will try to reduce his reliance on Arts Units of this type and gradually transition to gentler equivalents.

Leithanien's research into Originium Arts doesn't cover everything, and this thing is honestly beyond me. Even a Spire Caster wouldn't touch a suicidal contraption like this! Nobody clings to their own life harder than they do. ...Hm? You're saying an Ursus came up with it? Th-that actually makes a fair bit of sense.
—An unnamed Caster Operator

sections.title: Archive File 1
sections.text:
From Operator Viy's own account, and from the interviews the HR Department later conducted with operators of Ursus origin or with some knowledge of the situation in Ursus, we can roughly trace the origins of the "Freemen"—a distinctive group that long went unacknowledged by the Ursus authorities and unknown to the public at large.
The "Freemen" were, at first, a name that the founder of Ursus promised to the non-Ursus races then living within its borders. Igor offered them autonomy in exchange for their support in the war against the Hippogryph, yet once the nation was founded, that promise went unfulfilled year after year. What came instead was the forefathers of the Freemen being driven out into the wilderness under the name of "granted land," migrating endlessly before the Catastrophes, splintering apart into scattered settlements that shared nothing but a common name. In wartime they were conscripted as a source of soldiers; in peacetime they each tilled barren soil, subsisting at the barest possible level. Shut out from every advance of society, they in turn grew accustomed to using the very concept of "Freemen" to sever themselves from the Ursus state and people, and then struggled without end inside that seemingly "fated" isolation. As the lyrics of the song so often sung among them say, they show a stubborn insistence on seeking their road and their answers from their forebears, and from myth.

If everything is truly as he says, then the "Freemen" are indeed a striking microcosm of the Ursus nationalities question.
...Bearing in mind Semenko, the city the Royal Guards sank, it is quite possible that it too belonged to some branch of Elafia Freemen—which gives a far more intelligible explanation for why so total a disaster befell them so easily. A mobile city belonging to them and them alone should have been a conspicuous step forward for a people so long displaced, a home they had scarcely dared hope for; but given the long-standing policy of the Ursus authorities, which never permitted so much as a mention of the "Freemen," they could of course see it only as an attempt at secession.
This is not a defense of the reasonableness of Ursus's conduct. It is only that, looking back, even where these brutal events bear no direct connection to Rhodes Island, we ought to try to understand them and draw lessons from them. That will also be of considerable help in our future dealings with "Shchin," and indeed with the various factions of a no-longer-unified Ursus.
—Kal'tsit

sections.title: Archive File 2
sections.text:
Unlike the many lawful organizations that maintain a stable external partnership with Rhodes Island, "Shchin" is a paramilitary force in the midst of a transformation: not a mercenary outfit, and far beyond anything the words "security company" could define. It sits in a "gray zone" that Rhodes Island does not approach lightly, and the extent of our dealings with it must be judged with care. What is more, the attitude displayed by this leader of "Shchin," who moves about Rhodes Island Headquarters so freely, is equally ambiguous. Continued observation is advised.

[Audio Log]
"Oh, you mean the big Kuranta with the Ursus accent? He really is in the library all the time. Sometimes a book's too high up on the shelf and someone's already borrowed the ladder, and he'll offer to reach it for you—no, not just for the ladies. Anyone who needs a hand, he'll help. ...I know he's good-looking, but that's not why I remember him! He's covered in scars, on his neck, on his arms, and he never hides them. Anyone would notice, wouldn't they?"

[Borrowing Record]
The Angler's Codex
Diaphragmatic Breathing: Illustrated Edition
Drink the Wine You Made Yourself
Three Thousand Ursus Folk Songs
Toe Care for Steed Burdenbeasts
……
All of the above books and their accompanying videotapes were returned within the loan period, and nothing irregular was found.

[Audio Log]
"Ah, seems I got ahead of myself. I should have said something to one of you first. I heard in the canteen that your library has everything, so I thought I'd find some books with pictures in them and pass the time. It isn't like back in the village here, where someone would take your hands and show you how the family trades are done. Still, videotapes are handy enough. I've learned more in this one week than I used to in a whole month of summer rest.
"It's comfortable at Rhodes Island—that's why I keep coming. 'Shchin' is good too, of course, but when we stand down, every one of them has somewhere to be: back to Ursus to find family and children, or off with their pay to drink themselves blind. Men like us have precious little in the way of amusement. Once we're off the battlefield, we mostly just turn in circles where we stand. I'm trying to step out of that loop now. Call it setting them an example."

Operator Viy displays an extremely strong protectiveness toward his comrades in the "Shchin" legion, along with an almost unbelievable tolerance. As their leader, he seems untroubled by the possibility that such a manner will end in slack discipline and, one day, in the unit's destruction on the battlefield. "It's time we decided for ourselves how we're going to live," he said. Following assessment, they can be judged capable of taking responsibility for their own actions; and since we are the ones seeking cooperation, it is only right that we bear the necessary risk.

He takes the comrades under his command as his own responsibility, and yet gives them his trust without reserve. The degree of unity "Shchin" displays was seldom seen even among the most decorated legions of old Ursus. Stay on your guard, Doctor—but there is no need to judge these young people too harshly.
—Hellagur

sections.title: Archive File 3
sections.text:
After a period of observation, we noticed that Operator Viy is rather unfamiliar with paperwork. This does not mean he cannot read or write; he simply finds this sort of task "tiresome" and is averse to it, which makes him markedly inefficient whenever documents have to be handled on his own. Having also found that his second-in-command could offer little help in this regard, and in order to keep the partnership running smoothly, we assigned an operator from the reception desk with a talent for drafting documents to assist him during working hours with filing reports and similar matters. Operator Viy has taken well to the arrangement, and the two have already developed good working habits together.

[Report on the Disturbance at the Rhodes Island Headquarters Reception Desk]
It is reported that the banner bearing the words "I'm sorry, please forgive me" and the like, which appeared at the reception desk the day before, was sent by the family member of a patient who has long been in a financial dispute with Rhodes Island. It was meant to express approval of and gratitude for the service at the reception desk, and not to settle a lovers' quarrel. According to that family member, he now fully recognizes how inappropriate his earlier harassment was, and states that he will cooperate with Rhodes Island in settling the sums he owes as soon as possible.
In the follow-up interviews, the operator who had been at the reception desk when the banner went up gave his view of the matter: the credit was not his. He does not know who helped resolve this headache of a problem, but at the very least there is no longer someone standing at the reception desk shouting "Pay up!" and "Swindlers!" whom our security staff are nonetheless forbidden to remove by force. Order at the reception desk has been restored, which is wonderful news for everyone who comes to Rhodes Island.

...The moment I heard, I knew it was him! Always finding himself something to do. Once, we were camped out on the barrens alongside some other legions, and this orderly, still too young to shave, said that if we weren't Ursus then we were nothing. That night his boots went missing and turned up hanging from an old tree eight hundred meters off—soaked through, dripping without stop, heavy as stones! There were plenty more like that afterward. He never says a word about it, and he was never caught in the act, but everybody knows it was him. The truth is, we'd rather not make trouble. The army groups treat us as expendables, and what respect does an expendable need? Those below follow those above, that's all. But he won't swallow it. Every time someone comes at us, he bites back without fail.
—Oleg, Operator Viy's second-in-command

[Audio Log]
"Bad memory, what can you do. A grudge has to be repaid on the spot."

sections.title: Archive File 4
sections.text:
Some thirty years ago, a painter passing through a small village in the southern wilderness of Ursus painted a family portrait for a household that had borne an infant with a faint trace of Nightzmora blood. In the brushwork usually reserved for emperors and the Yurodstvo, he set down a family of four as ordinary as any in the wilds.
Some twenty years ago, the Catastrophe Messengers came. They pushed open the wooden fence and delivered the grim news of an approaching Catastrophe to the head of the village. It was a village that kept great herds of steed burdenbeasts, and all the villagers could have evacuated in time—all but one household of three, with a paralyzed father and a blind mother. Facing the dark press of people stepping into the house, the boy raised the curved blade that had broken on the battlefield along with his father's leg, and leveled it at the noble who walked out from behind the "Catastrophe Messengers." His hands did not tremble in the slightest. The noble asked: You've served. A child soldier? The boy said: Come no closer.
The "Catastrophe Messengers" took his parents away, the noble took the boy away, and the boy took away his elder sister's keepsake; the village itself was blasted apart by the Catastrophe that arrived on schedule the next day. In exchange for the protection given to his family, the boy entered a brutal training regimen, forcing his body to adapt to those violent weapons—he was thrown into the Empire's war factory, where the title of "War Caster" is granted to the "luckiest" one out of several hundred children.
A little over ten years ago, the boy was granted that title and began to make his mark in border frictions that no official record acknowledged: as a spy, as an assassin, as a commander, as the name he had finally been given. But when every disturbance he put down turned out to be the product of one faction purging another, and soldiers who ought to have devoted themselves to a great cause used civilians as their shield instead—he began to doubt, and then he turned.
A few years ago, having all but carved the flesh from his body, he finally left the army under a dead man's name, returned to a hometown already destroyed by a Catastrophe, and picked a broken picture frame out of the rubble. There he began to rebuild his life, and, drawing on what he had learned and thought through in the army, raised a company of his own.
Even now, though, he still wears the medal the army gave him—not because he believes in the conviction and loyalty it stands for, but simply because he cares to. If he cared to, he could of course sell it for a good price and buy his comrades a round. Nothing in this world holds still, he always thinks. When people ask why he left the army, he only says, "Got bored," and when someone finishes a little tune that is easy on the ear but filthy in its lyrics, he only says, "Sing it again."
The boy grew from a youth into a young man, and the young man, pulling along everyone who believes in him, keeps walking across the vast earth.

All right, I've heard it out, and it's not bad—but didn't you leave a setup with no payoff? And what exactly does this story have to do with Durins? Bring up Ursus one more time and I'll be asking you to leave.
—The organizer of the Durin Story Circle

sections.title: Promotion Record
sections.text:
Looking back on it now, every time the head of one village or another led his people out to "fight for Ursus," it was probably that first promise playing out all over again. Strange, isn't it? Taken for fools that many times and still never learning—it makes you feel that people like us are simply... meant to be treated that way. Damn it all.
Oleg is always saying that Vladimir really would have relented and granted us autonomy, and that he simply died too soon. But our parents' generation died off in droves not long after, and among those still alive, not one knows whether any of it ever happened at all. Besides, Silka has never believed it. Not by a hair.
But by now none of it matters. We have stopped looking to the Emperor, and the whole of Ursus no longer needs an emperor at all—so who is still waiting for a man who does not exist to make good on an old promise?
Picking sides, falling in line—everyone is sick of it, but I still believe I did the right thing back then. Perhaps when people look back on this history someday, they will find the name "Livonov" written there, or "Shchin." I only hope that when they leaf carefully through this outfit's record, they find that what really deserves remembering are those who chose to resist before us, earlier than any of us.
It was they who taught us: always to stand up and walk, and never to bend down and crawl. That is what the road of the "Freemen" truly is, a result that countless people paid for with their lives—
...It may not be the best road there is, but I will not fail it.
